claims.claim: Demolition of Pruitt-Igoe began in 1972 with a televised implosion, following federal (HUD) decisions to wind the project down.
claims.episode_span: the Department of Housing and Urban Development approved demolition in 1972
claims.supporting_quote: Demolition of the complex began in 1972 with a televised implosion of several of the buildings. Over the next four years, the rest of the complex was vacated and demolished.

claims.claim: Pruitt-Igoe consisted of 33 eleven-story towers designed by architect Minoru Yamasaki.
claims.episode_span: the first of the thirty-three eleven-story towers
claims.supporting_quote: The complex of 33 eleven-story high rises was designed in the modernist architectural style by Minoru Yamasaki .

claims.claim: The complex contained 2,870 apartments, matching the episode's figure of roughly 2,870 families housed.
claims.supporting_quote: The complex totaled 2,870 apartments (1,736 in Pruitt and 1,132 in Igoe [ 7 ] ) housing more than 10,000 people at full occupancy.

claims.claim: Construction began in 1951, the first tenants arrived in 1954-55, and the project initially cost about $36 million.
claims.episode_span: Construction began in 1951 and the complex was completed by 1955 at a cost of about $36 million.
claims.supporting_quote: Construction began in 1951. [ 24 ] Pruitt accepted its first tenants in November 1954, Igoe in July 1955. [ 25 ] When the two projects opened, they were one of the largest public housing developments in the country. [ 26 ] Even under federal cost-cutting regulations, Pruitt–Igoe initially cost $36 million

claims.claim: St. Louis public housing of this era was enabled and financed under the Housing Act of 1949.
claims.episode_span: The project grew out of the Housing Act of 1949
claims.supporting_quote: soon the situation was changed with the Housing Act of 1949 and Missouri state laws that provided co-financing of public housing projects.

claims.claim: The Housing Act of 1949 required local housing authorities to pay operating expenses from rental income, a structural cause of the maintenance collapse.
claims.episode_span: Maintenance budgets remained tied to rent collections, which fell as tenant incomes declined.
claims.supporting_quote: in particular the requirement of the Housing Act of 1949 that local housing authorities pay their expenses from rental income, which made them vulnerable to fiscal problems.

claims.claim: By around 1970 the majority of the complex (more than two-thirds) stood vacant, consistent with the episode's claim of over 60 percent vacancy by 1969.
claims.episode_span: By 1969 the complex was more than 60 percent vacant
claims.supporting_quote: Numerous initiatives to reverse the decline failed, and by 1970 more than two-thirds of the complex was vacant.

claims.episode_span: Architect Minoru Yamasaki, working with the firm Leinweber, Yamasaki & Hellmuth
